title: LiftDiff: Guided Discrete Diffusion for Quantum Code Construction

paper.title: LiftDiff: Guided Discrete Diffusion for Quantum Code Construction
paper.abstract:
Abstract The realization of fault-tolerant quantum computation relies on Quantum
Error-Correcting Codes (QECC). Of particular interest are codes that combine a high encoding rate with sufficient distance. Existing algebraic constructions, such as lifted product (LP) codes, build a large quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) code from a classical base matrix. In this work we introduce LiftDiff, a generative approach to the discovery of QECC. A discrete denoising diffusion model is trained to generate base matrices over the group algebra 𝔽 2 ​ [ ℤ ℓ ] \mathbb{F}_{2}[\mathbb{Z}_{\ell}] , which are then expanded into LP codes. The reverse diffusion process is guided by an energy function that evaluates quantum code properties, including girth, degree, sparsity and decoding performance, steering the sampler toward matrices that yield LP codes with favorable parameters. Our method discovers codes with parameters such as [ [ 169 , 13 , 11 ] ] [[169,13,11]] , [ [ 143 , 15 , 9 ] ] [[143,15,9]] , and [ [ 260 , 24 , 10 ] ] [[260,24,10]] , including a [ [ 247 , 19 , 14 ] ] [[247,19,14]] code that achieves the highest k ​ d 2 / n {kd^{2}}/{n} among the baselines. Moreover, several discovered codes outperform the Gross code across a broad range of the tested physical error rates under both code-capacity and circuit-level noise.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Quantum computing harnesses the laws of quantum mechanics to perform computation, giving rise to a fundamentally different computational paradigm from classical computing. This paradigm has the potential to provide substantial computational advantages for problems that are difficult to solve using classical methods ( Shor, 1997 ; Grover, 1996 ; Gidney and Ekerå, 2021 ; Feynman and others, 2018 ) . Quantum systems are, however, exceptionally noisy. The qubit, the elementary unit of quantum information, is coupled to its environment, and the resulting decoherence destroys the superpositions and phase relations on which the computation depends. Errors therefore accumulate before a computation of useful length can be completed. Quantum Error Correction (QEC) ( Calderbank and Shor, 1996 ) is thus indispensable for the realization of a quantum computer. Shor’s first QEC scheme ( Shor, 1995 ) demonstrated that these obstacles can be overcome, and that quantum information can be protected despite the impossibility of copying it and the continuous nature of the errors that afflict it. Considerable progress has been made since through the stabilizer formalism ( Gottesman, 1997 ) . Within the stabilizer framework, Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes ( Steane, 1996 ; Calderbank and Shor, 1996 ) form an important class of QECC constructed from two parity check matrices satisfying an orthogonality condition. Their structure separates the correction of bit-flip and phase-flip errors. Among the QEC schemes proposed, the surface code ( Kitaev, 1997 ; Bravyi and Kitaev, 1998 ; Kitaev, 2003 ; Dennis et al., 2002 ) has received the most attention. It tolerates a comparatively high physical error rate, and efficient decoders for it are available. Its drawback is the encoding rate. A surface code patch encodes a single logical qubit into a number of physical qubits that grows quadratically with the distance, so its encoding rate vanishes as the protection is increased. This has motivated the search for codes that keep the parity checks sparse while encoding many logical qubits in the same block. Classical LDPC codes combine sparse checks with efficient message-passing decoding and performance close to capacity, and recent years have seen sustained effort to create qLDPC codes ( Breuckmann and Eberhardt, 2021 ) , where the checks must in addition commute. The Hypergraph Product (HGP) ( Tillich and Zemor, 2014 ) provides a way to construct a qLDPC code using the parity check matrix of two classical codes. The LP construction replaces the binary entries of the base matrix with elements of a group algebra ( Panteleev and Kalachev, 2022 ) , allowing the constructed codes to achieve high encoding rate and distance. Among the most promising qLDPC constructions are the Bivariate Bicycle (BB) ( Bravyi et al., 2024 ) codes, whose CSS structure is defined through a pair of polynomials in the ring 𝔽 2 ​ [ x , y ] / ( x ℓ − 1 , y m − 1 ) \mathbb{F}_{2}[x,y]/(x^{\ell}-1,y^{m}-1) . Machine learning has been applied to a range of problems in the domain of quantum computing, such as quantum error decoding ( Wang and Tang, 2024 ; Bausch et al., 2024 ; Senior et al., 2026 ; Chamberland et al., 2026 ) and the design of QECC ( Olle et al., 2024 ; Su et al., 2025 ; Liu and Marquardt, 2026 ; Yan et al., 2026b ; Cruz-Benito et al., 2026 ) . Several approaches have been used to search the space of QECC. However, the discrete and combinatorial nature of the design space, together with the costly evaluation of the resulting codes, makes efficiently navigating this space challenging, particularly for larger constructions. Generative models offer another approach to this problem. A generative model can learn the underlying structure of the design space and produce new candidate constructions. In this work, we introduce LiftDiff, a generative approach to the discovery of QECC. Our method employs a discrete diffusion model trained on classical base matrices, which are subsequently used to construct quantum codes through LP. During inference, we guide the diffusion process using a set of energy functions designed to promote desirable code properties, steering the generation toward promising quantum code constructions. Our contributions are as follows: • We introduce, to the best of our knowledge, the first discrete diffusion framework for the generative construction of novel QECC. • We develop an energy-based guidance mechanism that operates throughout the reverse diffusion process, using differentiable quantum code properties to steer the generation toward base matrices with desirable properties after lifting. • LiftDiff can generate QECC with diverse combinations of code parameters, including [ [ 143 , 15 , 9 ] ] [[143,15,9]] , [ [ 260 , 24 , 10 ] ] [[260,24,10]] , and [ [ 169 , 13 , 11 ] ] [[169,13,11]] , as well as a [ [ 247 , 19 , 14 ] ] [[247,19,14]] code that achieves the highest k ​ d 2 / n kd^{2}/n among all baselines for a check weight ≤ 8 \leq 8 .

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Two major topics of research in QEC ( Roffe, 2019 ) are construction of quantum codes and the development of algorithms for decoding them, with recent work increasingly exploring machine learning as a tool for both tasks ( Wang and Tang, 2024 ; Alexeev et al., 2025 ; Krenn et al., 2023 ; Yan et al., 2026a ) . The construction of quantum codes has traditionally relied on algebraic and combinatorial methods, leading to a variety of code families with different trade-offs between rate, distance, and structural properties ( Bravyi et al., 2024 ; Tillich and Zemor, 2014 ; Panteleev and Kalachev, 2022 ; Breuckmann and Eberhardt, 2021 ; Kasai, 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Breuckmann and Terhal, 2016 ) . In terms of decoding, a wide range of decoders have been developed, such as Minimum Weight Perfect Matching, Union Find and Belief Propagation with Ordered Statistics Decoding (BP-OSD) ( Edmonds, 1965 ; Fowler, 2014 ; Delfosse and Nickerson, 2021 ; Panteleev and Kalachev, 2021 ) , as well as their variants ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Peled et al., 2026 ; Kwak et al., 2026 ) . More recently machine learning was also applied to develop neural decoders, spanning from Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) ( Gu et al., 2026 ) , Graph Neural Networks (GNN) ( Lange et al., 2025 ) to Transformers ( Blue et al., 2026 ; Zenati and Nachmani, 2026 ; Choukroun and Wolf, 2023 ) . Code Design was also explored using machine learning techniques, starting from reinforcement learning ( Olle et al., 2024 ; Nautrup et al., 2019 ; Su et al., 2025 ; Sella et al., 2026 ) , bayesian optimization ( Chengyu et al., 2026 ) to the usage of Large Language Models (LLMs) ( Cruz-Benito et al., 2026 ; Yan et al., 2026b ) .

sections.heading: 3 Background
sections.text: Quantum Foundations. A qubit is the basic unit of quantum information and can be described by a state: | ψ ⟩ = α ​ | 0 ⟩ + β ​ | 1 ⟩ |\psi\rangle=\alpha|0\rangle+\beta|1\rangle where α , β ∈ ℂ \alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{C} are probability amplitudes satisfying | α | 2 + | β | 2 = 1 |\alpha|^{2}+|\beta|^{2}=1 . An n n -qubit system is described by a state in a 2 n 2^{n} -dimensional Hilbert space. QECC exploit this structure to encode logical information into a larger set of physical qubits and protect it from noise. Stabilizer Formalism. The stabilizer formalism ( Gottesman, 1997 ) encodes quantum information by constraining an n n -qubit system to the simultaneous + 1 +1 eigenspace of a commuting set of Pauli operators within the Hilbert space ℋ 2 n \mathcal{H}_{2}^{n} . These operators are drawn from the n n -qubit Pauli group 𝒫 n \mathcal{P}_{n} , which consists of tensor products of single-qubit Pauli matrices. Errors manifest as operators that violate these symmetry constraints and can be identified through projective measurements that do not disturb the encoded logical information. Concretely, an [ [ n , k , d ] ] [[n,k,d]] quantum code encodes k k logical qubits into n n physical qubits with distance d d , the stabilizer code is specified by choosing m = n − k m=n-k independent generators { S i } i = 1 m \{S_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m} subject to the constraint that the group generated by these operators does not contain − I -I . The associated logical code space is given by C S = { | ψ ⟩ ∈ ℋ 2 n | S i | ψ ⟩ = | ψ ⟩ , ∀ i ∈ { 1 , … , m } } C_{S}=\left\{\,|\psi\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{2}^{n}\;\middle|\;S_{i}|\psi\rangle=|\psi\rangle,\ \forall i\in\{1,\dots,m\}\right\} . Measuring the stabilizer generators produces a binary syndrome that reflects the commutation relations between an error operator and the stabilizers, thereby enabling error identification while preserving the logical state, and a set of commuting stabilizer generators can be represented by a binary check matrix. CSS Codes. CSS codes are a subclass of stabilizer codes in which the stabilizer generators are decoupled into X X -type and Z Z -type checks. They can therefore be described by two binary matrices H X H_{X} and H Z H_{Z} , which must satisfy H X ​ H Z T = 0 H_{X}H_{Z}^{T}=0 to ensure that all stabilizer generators commute. In this case, the number of encoded logical qubits is: k = n − rank ​ ( H X ) − rank ​ ( H Z ) k=n-\text{rank}(H_{X})-\text{rank}(H_{Z}) Lifted Product Codes. The LP construction ( Panteleev and Kalachev, 2022 ) provides a systematic way of constructing CSS quantum codes from matrices over a group algebra. Let M 1 ∈ R m 1 × n 1 , M 2 ∈ R m 2 × n 2 , M_{1}\in R^{m_{1}\times n_{1}},\qquad M_{2}\in R^{m_{2}\times n_{2}}, (1) where R R is a group algebra over 𝔽 2 \mathbb{F}_{2} . The construction combines M 1 M_{1} and M 2 M_{2} and their involutions to form the CSS check matrices H X = [ M 1 ⊗ I n 2 | I m 1 ⊗ M 2 ∗ ] , H Z = [ I n 1 ⊗ M 2 | M 1 ∗ ⊗ I m 2 ] , H_{X}=\left[M_{1}\otimes I_{n_{2}}\;\middle|\;I_{m_{1}}\otimes M_{2}^{\ast}\right],\qquad H_{Z}=\left[I_{n_{1}}\otimes M_{2}\;\middle|\;M_{1}^{\ast}\otimes I_{m_{2}}\right], (2) where M ∗ M^{\ast} denotes the transpose together with the involution on the group algebra. By construction, the resulting matrices satisfy H X ​ H Z ∗ = 0 H_{X}H_{Z}^{\ast}=0 and therefore define a CSS code. For the cyclic group algebra R = 𝔽 2 ​ [ x ] / ( x ℓ − 1 ) R=\mathbb{F}_{2}[x]/(x^{\ell}-1) , each entry of the base matrices is a polynomial of degree less than ℓ \ell , and the lifted representation replaces each polynomial by its corresponding ℓ × ℓ \ell\times\ell circulant binary matrix. In this work, we consider the self-product case L ​ P ​ ( M , M ) LP(M,M) .

sections.heading: 4.1 Overview
sections.text: We propose a novel framework for constructing QECCs, specifically LP codes. LiftDiff does not operate directly on parity-check matrices, instead, it operates on a base matrix M ∈ R m × n M\in R^{m\times n} over the group algebra R = 𝔽 2 ​ [ ℤ ℓ ] R=\mathbb{F}_{2}[\mathbb{Z}_{\ell}] . The matrix M M then defines a quantum code via L ​ P ​ ( M , M ) LP(M,M) . The QECC search space is enormous, making the search for codes with specific properties challenging. Discrete diffusion is particularly well suited to this task for two reasons: (i) codes are binary, making discrete diffusion over binary instances a natural choice. (ii) The iterative nature of the diffusion process, together with its differentiable formulation, allows us to specify desired code properties and guide the diffusion process toward high-quality codes. Our pipeline consists of three stages: (i) Training. A discrete denoising diffusion model is trained to invert a bit-flip corruption process on base matrices drawn from a progressive-edge-growth (PEG) construction. The model learns what a sparse, high-girth base matrix looks like. (ii) Guided inference. The trained model is sampled in reverse, and at every denoising step the prediction is displaced along the gradient of an energy that scores the quantum code the current base matrix implies. The energy is computed by pushing the model’s continuous prediction through the LP. This stage produces batches of base matrices. This process is illustrated in Figure 1 (iii) Screening and certification. Every sample is expanded, verified to commute, and given its exact n n and k k , a relatively cheap distance bound ( Pryadko et al., 2022 ) is used to give a first indication of each code. The distance of the best codes is finally proven using Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) ( Cruz-Benito et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: 1. Decoding
sections.text: The first term asks that the generated code be easy to decode. We simulate the procedure of the decoding task. We sample a depolarizing error at physical rate p p under the code-capacity noise model. Writing e X , e Z ∈ { 0 , 1 } n e_{X},e_{Z}\in\{0,1\}^{n} for the two components of that error, the syndromes are formed against the continuous check matrices through equation 15 , s Z = par ⁡ ( e X ​ H Z 𝖳 ) , s X = par ⁡ ( e Z ​ H X 𝖳 ) . s_{Z}=\mathrm{par}\bigl(e_{X}H_{Z}^{\mathsf{T}}\bigr),\qquad s_{X}=\mathrm{par}\bigl(e_{Z}H_{X}^{\mathsf{T}}\bigr). sections.heading: 4.5 Screening and exact distance certification
sections.text: Generation returns batches of candidate base matrices. Each generated sample is expanded into the corresponding parity-check matrices H X H_{X} and H Z H_{Z} , which are first verified to satisfy the commutation condition H X ​ H Z 𝖳 = 0 H_{X}H_{Z}^{\mathsf{T}}=0 . For each valid code, compute its block length n n and number of logical qubits k = n − rank ⁡ H X − rank ⁡ H Z k=n-\operatorname{rank}H_{X}-\operatorname{rank}H_{Z} . During evaluation, the distance of each generated code is estimated using the open-source upper-bound tool of Pryadko et al. (2022) . The generated codes are subsequently ranked according to their n n , k k , distance upper bound and maximum check weight, where the latter is defined as the heaviest row weight across H X H_{X} and H Z H_{Z} . As exact quantum-code distance computation is NP-hard in general ( Kapshikar and Kundu, 2023 ) , we use MILP to compute the exact distance of the final candidates, using the implementation of Cruz-Benito et al. (2026) .

sections.heading: 5.1 Experimental setup
sections.text: Our experimental evaluation follows the pipeline introduced in Section 4 . We employ the network described in Section 4.2 as the denoiser in the diffusion process. The architecture consists of L L layers, h h attention heads, and an embedding dimension d d . While the exact configuration varies per setting, the parameter count is approximately 10.7 10.7 M, depending slightly on ℓ \ell . Training samples are generated on the fly. Due to the lack of relevant data and to provide a more structured training distribution than uniformly random matrices, each sample is constructed in two steps. First, a binary m × n m\times n support is generated using a PEG procedure ( Hu et al., 2005 ) . Second, each nonzero entry in the support is assigned a random polynomial with weight w ∼ Uniform ⁡ { 1 , … , w max } w\sim\mathrm{Uniform}\{1,\dots,w_{\max}\} , with w w positions selected uniformly. We treat w max w_{\max} as a hyperparameter, with the goal of providing the model with a basic sparse structural prior. The forward corruption process spans T = 100 T=100 steps under a cosine schedule, with β t \beta_{t} ranging from 10 − 4 10^{-4} to 2 × 10 − 2 2\times 10^{-2} . We train the model for 750 750 epochs using AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017 ) with a batch size of 16 16 . In each epoch, 4096 4096 base matrices are generated using the PEG sampler. The peak learning rate is 10 − 4 10^{-4} with a weight decay of 10 − 4 10^{-4} . The learning rate undergoes a linear warmup over the first 20 20 epochs before annealing to zero via cosine decay. Gradients are clipped to a maximum norm of 1.0 1.0 , and the degree term in the loss function of equation 11 is weighted by λ deg = 3.0 \lambda_{\deg}=3.0 . Training is performed on a single NVIDIA L40 GPU, with each epoch taking approximately 5 5 seconds. During inference, each run generates a batch of 64 64 samples using the guided reverse process defined in equation 13 . Each run is initialized with a specific base geometry ( m , n , ℓ ) (m,n,\ell) , a target column weight d v d_{v} , and a maximum polynomial weight w max w_{\max} . The guidance scale and the hyperparameters of all energy terms are tuned individually for each run. Complete configurations for all generated results are provided in Appendix C . sections.heading: 5.2 Generated codes
sections.text: We gathered 32 codes produced by LiftDiff, detailed in the accompanying Table 1 . The discovered codes cover a broad range of [ [ n , k , d ] ] [[n,k,d]] parameters, with block lengths ( n n ) ranging from 65 to 730, and distances ( d d ) between 5 and 14. Our construction achieves high encoding rates ( k / n k/n ), reaching up to 0.310 while keeping the maximum check weight ( w chk w_{\text{chk}} ) within a range of 5 to 12. Several codes demonstrate a favorable balance between encoding rate, distance, and hardware-friendly check weights (for example 6, 13–16 and 18). Panel (a) illustrates the trade-off between d d and k / n k/n . Our codes achieve high encoding rates, extending beyond 0.30. Panel (b) evaluates the overall code efficiency k ​ d 2 / n kd^{2}/n as a function of the block length n n . The results demonstrate that our method achieves high code efficiency across a range of block lengths. sections.heading: 5.3 Logical error rate
sections.text: To evaluate the error-correction performance of the codes generated by LiftDiff, we measure the code-capacity logical error rate (LER) as a function of the physical error rate p p as illustrated in Figure 3(a) . We consider independent X X errors occurring on each qubit with probability p p , and decode the resulting Z Z -syndrome using BP-OSD with product-sum BP for 20 iterations, followed by OSD with CS order 7, following the simulation procedure of Cruz-Benito et al. (2026) . For each value of p p , we generate 10 6 10^{6} independent error samples. Figure 3(a) shows the resulting LER curves for four codes generated by LiftDiff, together with the [ [ 144 , 12 , 12 ] ] \left[\left[144,12,12\right]\right] code for comparison. The [ [ 260 , 24 , 10 ] ] [[260,24,10]] and [ [ 169 , 13 , 11 ] ] [[169,13,11]] codes stay below the [ [ 144 , 12 , 12 ] ] [[144,12,12]] curve over almost the entire range, up to p = 0.04 p=0.04 , and only meet the baseline at p = 0.05 p=0.05 . The [ [ 143 , 15 , 9 ] ] [[143,15,9]] code is below it for p ≤ 0.02 p\leq 0.02 , matches it at p = 0.03 p=0.03 and rises above it beyond that. The gap is widest at low physical error rates: at p = 0.01 p=0.01 the [ [ 260 , 24 , 10 ] ] [[260,24,10]] code reaches an LER about twenty times lower than the [ [ 144 , 12 , 12 ] ] [[144,12,12]] code, while [ [ 143 , 15 , 9 ] ] [[143,15,9]] and [ [ 169 , 13 , 11 ] ] [[169,13,11]] are lower by factors of about nine and four. This makes the result of the [ [ 260 , 24 , 10 ] ] [[260,24,10]] code notable, since it reaches the lowest curve while encoding twice as many logical qubits as the [ [ 144 , 12 , 12 ] ] [[144,12,12]] code. sections.heading: 6 Model Analysis
sections.text: To further evaluate the proposed method, we conducted additional experiments. In Figure 3(b) , we present two runs initialized with the same seed, one without the guidance mechanism and the other with guidance. The curve shows the percentage of differing matrices between the two batches throughout the denoising process. Since the two runs are otherwise identical, each matrix in one batch can be paired with the corresponding matrix in the other batch, allowing us to directly measure the effect of guidance on each sample. As the denoising process progresses, the percentage of differing matrices increases, such that by the end of the process, there are almost no identical matrices between the two batches. In Figure 3(c) , we examine how this divergence is reflected in the distance and maximum check weight of the resulting codes. The target region corresponds to high distance and a maximum check weight between 6 and 10, as indicated by the marked boundaries. This region is predominantly occupied by codes generated with the guidance mechanism, aggregated across multiple random seeds. In contrast, majority of codes generated by the model without guidance are concentrated at lower maximum check weights, but also exhibit lower distances. This separation indicates that, while the unguided model tends to generate codes with lower check weights, the guidance mechanism steers the generation process toward regions of the search space that are more relevant to our target criteria, allowing us to reach codes with higher distances while maintaining a maximum check weight in the desired range.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we introduced LiftDiff, the first discrete diffusion model designed for generating QECC, specifically, LP codes. Our framework demonstrates that generative models provide a highly effective strategy for navigating the vast search space of QECC. The experimental results yield robust codes characterized by competitive encoding rates, code distances, and low LER.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.25213v1 [quant-ph] 18 Oct 2026 LiftDiff: Guided Discrete Diffusion for Quantum Code Construction Yotam Peled Eliya Nachmani Affiliation: School of Electrical And Computer Engineering Affiliation: Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, Israel Affiliation: peledyot@post.bgu.ac.il, eliyanac@bgu.ac.il Abstract The realization of fault-tolerant quantum computation relies on Quantum Error-Correcting Codes (QECC). Of particular interest are codes that combine a high encoding rate with sufficient distance. Existing algebraic constructions, such as lifted product (LP) codes, build a large quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) code from a classical base matrix. In this work we introduce LiftDiff, a generative approach to the discovery of QECC. A discrete denoising diffusion model is trained to generate base matrices over the group algebra 𝔽 2 ​ [ ℤ ℓ ] \mathbb{F}_{2}[\mathbb{Z}_{\ell}] , which are then expanded into LP codes. The reverse diffusion process is guided by an energy function that evaluates quantum code properties, including girth, degree, sparsity and decoding performance, steering the sampler toward matrices that yield LP codes with favorable parameters. Our method discovers codes with parameters such as [ [ 169 , 13 , 11 ] ] [[169,13,11]] , [ [ 143 , 15 , 9 ] ] [[143,15,9]] , and [ [ 260 , 24 , 10 ] ] [[260,24,10]] , including a [ [ 247 , 19 , 14 ] ] [[247,19,14]] code that achieves the highest k ​ d 2 / n {kd^{2}}/{n} among the baselines. Moreover, several discovered codes outperform the Gross code across a broad range of the tested physical error rates under both code-capacity and circuit-level noise. 1 Introduction Quantum computing harnesses the laws of quantum mechanics to perform computation, giving rise to a fundamentally different computational paradigm from classical computing. This paradigm has the potential to provide substantial computational advantages for problems that are difficult to solve using classical methods ( Shor, 1997 ; Grover, 1996 ; Gidney and Ekerå, 2021 ; Feynman and others, 2018 ) . Quantum systems are, however, exceptionally noisy. The qubit, the elementary unit of quantum information, is coupled to its environment, and the resulting decoherence destroys the superpositions and phase relations on which the computation depends. Errors therefore accumulate before a computation of useful length can be completed. Quantum Error Correction (QEC) ( Calderbank and Shor, 1996 ) is thus indispensable for the realization of a quantum computer. Shor’s first QEC scheme ( Shor, 1995 ) demonstrated that these obstacles can be overcome, and that quantum information can be protected despite the impossibility of copying it and the continuous nature of the errors that afflict it. Considerable progress has been made since through the stabilizer formalism ( Gottesman, 1997 ) . Within the stabilizer framework, Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes ( Steane, 1996 ; Calderbank and Shor, 1996 ) form an important class of QECC constructed from two parity check matrices satisfying an orthogonality condition. Their structure separates the correction of bit-flip and phase-flip errors. Among the QEC schemes proposed, the surface code ( Kitaev, 1997 ; Bravyi and Kitaev, 1998 ; Kitaev, 2003 ; Dennis et al., 2002 ) has received the most attention. It tolerates a comparatively high physical error rate, and efficient decoders for it are available. Its drawback is the encoding rate. A surface code patch encodes a single logical qubit into a number of physical qubits that grows quadratically with the distance, so its encoding rate vanishes as the protection is increased. This has motivated the search for codes that keep the parity checks sparse while encoding many logical qubits in the same block. Classical LDPC codes combine sparse checks with efficient message-passing decoding and performance close to capacity, and recent years have seen sustained effort to create qLDPC codes ( Breuckmann and Eberhardt, 2021 ) , where the checks must in addition commute. The Hypergraph Product (HGP) ( Tillich and Zemor, 2014 ) provides a way to construct a qLDPC code using the parity check matrix of two classical codes. The LP construction replaces the binary entries of the base matrix with elements of a group algebra ( Panteleev and Kalachev, 2022 ) , allowing the constructed codes to achieve high encoding rate and distance. Among the most promising qLDPC constructions are the Bivariate Bicycle (BB) ( Bravyi et al., 2024 ) codes, whose CSS structure is defined through a pair of polynomials in the ring 𝔽 2 ​ [ x , y ] / ( x ℓ − 1 , y m − 1 ) \mathbb{F}_{2}[x,y]/(x^{\ell}-1,y^{m}-1) . Machine learning has been applied to a range of problems in the domain of quantum computing, such as quantum error decoding ( Wang and Tang, 2024 ; Bausch et al., 2024 ; Senior et al., 2026 ; Chamberland et al., 2026 ) and the design of QECC ( Olle et al., 2024 ; Su et al., 2025 ; Liu and Marquardt, 2026 ; Yan et al., 2026b ; Cruz-Benito et al., 2026 ) . Several approaches have been used to search the space of QECC. However, the discrete and combinatorial nature of the design space, together with the costly evaluation of the resulting codes, makes efficiently navigating this space challenging, particularly for larger constructions. Generative models offer another approach to this problem. A generative model can learn the underlying structure of the design space and produce new candidate constructions. In this work, we introduce LiftDiff, a generative approach to the discovery of QECC. Our method employs a discrete diffusion model trained on classical base matrices, which are subsequently used to construct quantum codes through LP. During inference, we guide the diffusion process using a set of energy functions designed to promote desirable code properties, steering the generation toward promising quantum code constructions. Our contributions are as follows: • We introduce, to the best of our knowledge, the first discrete diffusion framework for the generative construction of novel QECC. • We develop an energy-based guidance mechanism that operates throughout the reverse diffusion process, using differentiable quantum code properties to steer the generation toward base matrices with desirable properties after lifting. • LiftDiff can generate QECC with diverse combinations of code parameters, including [ [ 143 , 15 , 9 ] ] [[143,15,9]] , [ [ 260 , 24 , 10 ] ] [[260,24,10]] , and [ [ 169 , 13 , 11 ] ] [[169,13,11]] , as well as a [ [ 247 , 19 , 14 ] ] [[247,19,14]] code that achieves the highest k ​ d 2 / n kd^{2}/n among all baselines for a check weight ≤ 8 \leq 8 . 2 Related Work Two major topics of research in QEC ( Roffe, 2019 ) are construction of quantum codes and the development of algorithms for decoding them, with recent work increasingly exploring machine learning as a tool for both tasks ( Wang and Tang, 2024 ; Alexeev et al., 2025 ; Krenn et al., 2023 ; Yan et al., 2026a ) . The construction of quantum codes has traditionally relied on algebraic and combinatorial methods, leading to a variety of code families with different trade-offs between rate, distance, and structural properties ( Bravyi et al., 2024 ; Tillich and Zemor, 2014 ; Panteleev and Kalachev, 2022 ; Breuckmann and Eberhardt, 2021 ; Kasai, 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Breuckmann and Terhal, 2016 ) . In terms of decoding, a wide range of decoders have been developed, such as Minimum Weight Perfect Matching, Union Find and Belief Propagation with Ordered Statistics Decoding (BP-OSD) ( Edmonds, 1965 ; Fowler, 2014 ; Delfosse and Nickerson, 2021 ; Panteleev and Kalachev, 2021 ) , as well as their variants ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Peled et al., 2026 ; Kwak et al., 2026 ) . More recently machine learning was also applied to develop neural decoders, spanning from Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) ( Gu et al., 2026 ) , Graph Neural Networks (GNN) ( Lange et al., 2025 ) to Transformers ( Blue et al., 2026 ; Zenati and Nachmani, 2026 ; Choukroun and Wolf, 2023 ) . Code Design was also explored using machine learning techniques, starting from reinforcement learning ( Olle et al., 2024 ; Nautrup et al., 2019 ; Su et al., 2025 ; Sella et al., 2026 ) , bayesian optimization ( Chengyu et al., 2026 ) to the usage of Large Language Models (LLMs) ( Cruz-Benito et al., 2026 ; Yan et al., 2026b ) . 3 Background Quantum Foundations. A qubit is the basic unit of quantum information and can be described by a state: | ψ ⟩ = α ​ | 0 ⟩ + β ​ | 1 ⟩ |\psi\rangle=\alpha|0\rangle+\beta|1\rangle where α , β ∈ ℂ \alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{C} are probability amplitudes satisfying | α | 2 + | β | 2 = 1 |\alpha|^{2}+|\beta|^{2}=1 . An n n -qubit system is described by a state in a 2 n 2^{n} -dimensional Hilbert space. QECC exploit this structure to encode logical information into a larger set of physical qubits and protect it from noise. Stabilizer Formalism. The stabilizer formalism ( Gottesman, 1997 ) encodes quantum information by constraining an n n -qubit system to the simultaneous + 1 +1 eigenspace of a commuting set of Pauli operators within the Hilbert space ℋ 2 n \mathcal{H}_{2}^{n} . These operators are drawn from the n n -qubit Pauli group 𝒫 n \mathcal{P}_{n} , which consists of tensor products of single-qubit Pauli matrices. Errors manifest as operators that violate these symmetry constraints and can be identified through projective measurements that do not disturb the encoded logical information. Concretely, an [ [ n , k , d ] ] [[n,k,d]] quantum code encodes k k logical qubits into n n physical qubits with distance d d , the stabilizer code is specified by choosing m = n − k m=n-k independent generators { S i } i = 1 m \{S_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m} subject to the constraint that the group generated by these operators does not contain − I -I . The associated logical code space is given by C S = { | ψ ⟩ ∈ ℋ 2 n | S i | ψ ⟩ = | ψ ⟩ , ∀ i ∈ { 1 , … , m } } C_{S}=\left\{\,|\psi\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{2}^{n}\;\middle|\;S_{i}|\psi\rangle=|\psi\rangle,\ \forall i\in\{1,\dots,m\}\right\} . Measuring the stabilizer generators produces a binary syndrome that reflects the commutation relations between an error operator and the stabilizers, thereby enabling error identification while preserving the logical state, and a set of commuting stabilizer generators can be represented by a binary check matrix. CSS Codes. CSS codes are a subclass of stabilizer codes in which the stabilizer generators are decoupled into X X -type and Z Z -type checks. They can therefore be described by two binary matrices H X H_{X} and H Z H_{Z} , which must satisfy H X ​ H Z T = 0 H_{X}H_{Z}^{T}=0 to ensure that all stabilizer generators commute. In this case, the number of encoded logical qubits is: k = n − rank ​ ( H X ) − rank ​ ( H Z ) k=n-\text{rank}(H_{X})-\text{rank}(H_{Z}) Lifted Product Codes. The LP construction ( Panteleev and Kalachev, 2022 ) provides a systematic way of constructing CSS quantum codes from matrices over a group algebra. Let M 1 ∈ R m 1 × n 1 , M 2 ∈ R m 2 × n 2 , M_{1}\in R^{m_{1}\times n_{1}},\qquad M_{2}\in R^{m_{2}\times n_{2}}, (1) where R R is a group algebra over 𝔽 2 \mathbb{F}_{2} . The construction combines M 1 M_{1} and M 2 M_{2} and their involutions to form the CSS check matrices H X = [ M 1 ⊗ I n 2 | I m 1 ⊗ M 2 ∗ ] , H Z = [ I n 1 ⊗ M 2 | M 1 ∗ ⊗ I m 2 ] , H_{X}=\left[M_{1}\otimes I_{n_{2}}\;\middle|\;I_{m_{1}}\otimes M_{2}^{\ast}\right],\qquad H_{Z}=\left[I_{n_{1}}\otimes M_{2}\;\middle|\;M_{1}^{\ast}\otimes I_{m_{2}}\right], (2) where M ∗ M^{\ast} denotes the transpose together with the involution on the group algebra. By construction, the resulting matrices satisfy H X ​ H Z ∗ = 0 H_{X}H_{Z}^{\ast}=0 and therefore define a CSS code. For the cyclic group algebra R = 𝔽 2 ​ [ x ] / ( x ℓ − 1 ) R=\mathbb{F}_{2}[x]/(x^{\ell}-1) , each entry of the base matrices is a polynomial of degree less than ℓ \ell , and the lifted representation replaces each polynomial by its corresponding ℓ × ℓ \ell\times\ell circulant binary matrix. In this work, we consider the self-product case L ​ P ​ ( M , M ) LP(M,M) . 4 Method 4.1 Overview We propose a novel framework for constructing QECCs, specifically LP codes. LiftDiff does not operate directly on parity-check matrices, instead, it operates on a base matrix M ∈ R m × n M\in R^{m\times n} over the group algebra R = 𝔽 2 ​ [ ℤ ℓ ] R=\mathbb{F}_{2}[\mathbb{Z}_{\ell}] . The matrix M M then defines a quantum code via L ​ P ​ ( M , M ) LP(M,M) . The QECC search space is enormous, making the search for codes with specific properties challenging. Discrete diffusion is particularly well suited to this task for two reasons: (i) codes are binary, making discrete diffusion over binary instances a natural choice. (ii) The iterative nature of the diffusion process, together with its differentiable formulation, allows us to specify desired code properties and guide the diffusion process toward high-quality codes. Our pipeline consists of three stages: (i) Training. A discrete denoising diffusion model is trained to invert a bit-flip corruption process on base matrices drawn from a progressive-edge-growth (PEG) construction. The model learns what a sparse, high-girth base matrix looks like. (ii) Guided inference. The trained model is sampled in reverse, and at every denoising step the prediction is displaced along the gradient of an energy that scores the quantum code the current base matrix implies. The energy is computed by pushing the model’s continuous prediction through the LP. This stage produces batches of base matrices. Every sample is expanded, verified to commute, and given its exact n n and k k , a relatively cheap distance bound ( Pryadko et al., 2022 ) is used to give a first indication of each code.
